Article Title: Pakistan forces accused of quadcopter blast that killed 2 children in Balochistan
Article Text:
Pakistan forces accused of quadcopter link

A blast in Balochistan's Panjgur district killed two children and left three others injured, The Balochistan Post reported. The incident took place in Fateh Ali Bazaar in Gowargo tehsil, where the children had been playing.According to the report, the children noticed an unidentified object hanging from a tree. The object exploded after it was disturbed, killing two boys aged nine and 10. Three other boys, aged seven, nine and 12, were injured.The nature of the device that caused the explosion remains unclear.However, local sources alleged that it was connected to a quadcopter operated by Pakistani security forces. One source also claimed that explosives had been attached to a military quadcopter and placed in the area.The source further alleged that local journalists were later told to describe the incident as a hand-grenade blast or an explosion involving another device.The Panjgur incident comes amid other allegations of civilian casualties involving military drones and quadcopters in Balochistan.On September 24, four young men were killed and two others injured in an alleged military drone strike in Balicha, Kech, according to The Balochistan Post.Families of those killed said the men had gone there for a picnic and denied claims that they were militants.The incident triggered a boycott of courts across Makran, while lawyers called for an independent probe into the deaths.Earlier on September 18, five civilians were reportedly injured in alleged quadcopter attacks in Balochabad and Bullo in the Mand area, the report said.
Article Summary: Blast in Balochistan's Panjgur district killed two children and left three others injured. Local sources alleged that it was connected to a quadcopter operated by Pakistani security forces. Incident comes amid other allegations of civilian casualties involving military drones and quadcopters.

Article Title: In 1993, Bob Hope sold his 2,308-acre California ranch to the National Park Service for $16.7 million; the deal turned his former property into federal parkland and expanded protected land to about 20
Article Text:
Bob HopePhoto: Wikimedia Common

A ranch in the Simi Hills

Part of a larger conservation puzzle

How the purchase came together

From private ranch to public recreation area

A legacy of land and conservation

In 1993, comedian and entertainer Bob Hope sold his 2,308-acre Jordan Ranch in eastern Ventura County to the National Park Service for $16.7 million. The acquisition added the rugged, oak-dotted property to the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, bringing the park service’s holdings in the recreation area to about 20,400 acres, as per a report by Parade. Officials described Jordan Ranch as the crown jewel of the Simi Hills and the largest single acquisition within the recreation area at the time, according to various reports and project summaries. Read on to know more about it here:Jordan Ranch sits in the Simi Hills east of Thousand Oaks, a landscape of rolling meadows, oak-lined canyons and grassy flats. The property includes Palo Comado Canyon and China Flat, areas that were praised for their natural beauty even before they became public parkland. Descriptions from the period refer to China Flat as a spectacular vantage point overlooking tiers of distant mountains, as per LA Times.Before the sale, the ranch had been eyed for development. Earlier proposals included luxury homes and a world-class golf course on parts of the property. The 1993 transaction ended those plans and ensured that the land would be preserved as open space. Park officials said the ranch would open for recreational use within four to six months, welcoming hikers, bikers and equestrians to terrain that had been privately held for decades.The sale also connected Jordan Ranch to adjacent protected land. The 2,308-acre tract abuts the 2,150-acre Cheeseboro Canyon property, which was already part of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. As per LA Times, superintendents described the acquisition as preserving a key part of a wildlife corridor that runs from Simi Valley to the Pacific Ocean, allowing deer, bobcats and other large mammals to move between mountain ranges.The Jordan Ranch deal did not happen in isolation. It was tied to broader negotiations involving other Hope-owned properties and a major housing project known as Ahmanson Ranch. Under conditions set by the Ventura County Board of Supervisors, the Ahmanson development could not proceed until Hope’s other mountain tracts became public parkland. Those properties included the 4,369-acre Runkle Ranch near Simi Valley and the 339-acre Corral Canyon in Malibu.In 1990, Hope had signed an agreement to transfer about 5,700 acres of mountain property at three sites to a state parks agency for a below-market $20 million. That deal included Runkle Ranch, Corral Canyon and portions of Jordan Ranch, and it was described as one of the largest and most significant parkland transactions in recent Southern California history. The 1993 sale of Jordan Ranch to the National Park Service fulfilled part of that broader conservation framework. By 1991, a more complex arrangement had emerged. Hope agreed to a plan that would combine two giant housing projects near Simi Valley and turn more than 10,000 acres of mountain property into public parkland. Under that consolidated plan, park agencies would receive parklands worth between $120 million and $150 million, while Hope would sell 7,363 acres for a below-market $29.5 million. The Jordan Ranch sale in 1993 was a key step in making that vision a reality, as per reports.The final Jordan Ranch transaction followed more than five years of intense and ever-shifting negotiations. State park officials scrambled at times to secure federal funds before they expired, fearing the money might be redirected to other parkland acquisitions. At one point, the National Park Service signaled its intent to buy the 314-acre Paramount Ranch property in Agoura using money that had been set aside for Hope properties, adding urgency to the Jordan Ranch talks.Parade.com noted that Joseph T. Edmiston, executive director of the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, played a central role in engineering the $16.7 million purchase. He announced, as per the report, that the acquisition in June 1993 and said Hope would receive the Park Service’s payment within the next few days. Escrow was expected to close that Friday or the following Monday, marking the end of a long process that had involved developers, conservationists and local officials.The purchase price was widely reported as $16.7 million for the 2,308-acre ranch. That figure represented a significant investment in open space at a time when development pressure in the region was high. Edmiston described Jordan Ranch as a very critical parcel because it represented another key swath of protected wildlife habitat in the Santa Monica Mountains.Once the sale closed, the National Park Service began planning how to manage the newly acquired land. Officials said getting the parkland ready for the public would cost about $120,000 in the first year, covering ranger patrols, road improvements, and the installation of gates and parking spaces. Blueprints for amenities such as restrooms, picnic tables and parking lots had not yet been drawn up at the time of the announcement.The entire property, including oak-lined Palo Comado Canyon and sage-carpeted China Flat, was expected to open for recreational use within months. Park officials anticipated that hikers, bikers and equestrians would quickly discover the rugged ranch, which had once been slated for luxury homes and a golf course. The opening marked a transition from private ownership to a space where the public could explore canyons, meadows and ridgelines that had been off limits for decades.The acquisition also had implications for nearby development. The Ahmanson Ranch project, a $1 billion plan to create a mini-city of 8,600 residents, remained contingent on Hope’s other properties becoming public parkland. The Jordan Ranch sale was a major accomplishment, but officials said the burden now fell on Ahmanson Land Co. to deliver two other Hope properties to park agencies if it wanted to build the housing project.Bob Hope was one of the largest private landowners in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area during the early 1990s. His holdings included Jordan Ranch, Runkle Ranch and Corral Canyon, along with other parcels in the region. The series of deals he entered into with park agencies put thousands of acres into public ownership and helped shape the recreation area’s boundaries.In addition to the Jordan Ranch sale, Hope donated 360 acres of his Conejo Valley land to the Conejo Recreation and Park District. That property became the Hope Nature Preserve, a protected open-space area named in his honor. The combination of sales and donations ensured that a significant portion of his mountain land would remain undeveloped and accessible to the public.Today, Jordan Ranch is part of the Cheeseboro and Palo Comado Canyons Park section of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. The recreation area has grown to more than 150,000 acres and is often described as the world’s largest urban national park. The 1993 sale of Jordan Ranch remains a landmark moment in that growth, turning a celebrity-owned ranch into federal parkland and expanding protected land to about 20,400 acres at the time.
Article Summary: In 1993, comedian and entertainer Bob Hope sold his 2,308-acre Jordan Ranch to the National Park Service for $16.7 million. The acquisition added the rugged, oak-dotted property to the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. The sale was tied to broader negotiations involving other Hope-owned properties and a major housing project.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg to Yvon Chouinard: Six of the world's richest people who are not leaving their billions worth of fortune to their children
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg

Laurene Powell Jobs

After the death of the famous founder, she inherited a fortune worth $14.9 billion but is not planning on giving it away to her three children

Michael Bloomberg

Bill Gates

Warren Buffet

Passing down mass amounts of money "just because they came out of the right womb" is an "antisocial act," he said.

Yvon Chouinard

"Money won't make success; the freedom to make it will," said Nelson Mandela. For numerous billionaires across the world, money was not a given; they began with nothing and worked hard enough to now own everything. For their families and friends, they have made sure money is never a factor to consider when living life. But as important as financial stability is to a person, so is the will to do something on their own, create something of their own. And that is one thing the wealthy seem to understand, since they seem to be implementing it in their own children as well.In the next two decades, the heirs of the world's richest are set to become even richer. An estimated $84 trillion is expected to be passed down in what has been deemed the largest-ever transfer of intergenerational wealth. However, not all billionaires seem to be on board. From Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to Patagonia founder Yvon Chouinard, some have decided against leaving their fortunes to their children, according to a recent report by Observer. Here's a look at the who's and who's of the world that decided not to offer their wealth to their kids.Mark Zuckerberg started Facebook, now Meta Platforms, from a dorm room at Harvard University. The 42-year-old's $199 billion fortune is connected to his 13% ownership of the company's stock. However, he and his wife Priscilla Chan intend to give away 99% of their Meta shares. Shortly after the birth of their first child in 2015, the couple announced their plans to use the funds to promote equality, medical innovations and education through the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, which has committed more than $7.2 billion in grants since beginning in 2015.“Our society has an obligation to invest now to improve the lives of all those coming into this world, not just those already here,” said Zuckerberg at the time.Laurene Powell Jobs is the wife of late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs. After the death of the famous founder, she inherited a fortune worth $14.9 billion but is not planning on giving it away to her three children. “I’m not interested in legacy wealth buildings, and my children know that,” she told The New York Times in 2020. “Steve wasn’t interested in that. If I live long enough, it ends with me.”Powell Jobs instead plans to distribute her money "in ways that uplift individuals and communities in a sustainable way." Much of this has taken place through her umbrella organisation Emerson Collective, an organisation focused on impact investing, philanthropy and advocacy around environmental justice, health, immigration and education. It is estimated that Powell Jobs has already donated more than $2 billion to charitable causes through this fund. She has also reportedly been selling roughly 10% of her Disney shares each year since 2011. In addition, she pledged in 2021 to donate $3.5 billion over 10 years to organizations developing innovative solutions to climate change, a commitment she is fulfilling through the Waverley Street Foundation.Michael Bloomberg is the founder of Bloomberg L.P., an empire that constitutes his eponymous media businesses and the Bloomberg Terminal, a financial data service. Despite owning a fortune worth $109 billion, he doesn't intend to pass on his wealth to his two children. Instead in 2025, he announced that his company will eventually be given to a trust intended to finance Bloomberg Philanthropies, his charitable foundation. “When I die, the foundation inherits the company,” said Bloomberg during a summit in September 2023. “They, because of the tax laws, will have to get rid of it, sell it someplace or other over the first five years,” he added. The billionaire has also previously advocated against wealthy families hiring their own children, stating in 2016 that he would never let his daughters work for his company as it would be unfair to other employees.Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in 1975 after Gates dropped out of Harvard University. Through years of effort, the now 70-years-old has amassed an estimated fortune of $108.5 billion. This is despite him having given away most of his Microsoft stakes to fund his philanthropic Gates Foundation.Still, his three children do not expect to receive much of it. The billionaire has long maintained that his kids will be receiving only a "miniscule portion" of his wealth and will "have to find their own way." In a 2017 Reddit AMA, Gates reportedly noted that “leaving kids massive amounts of money is not a favor to them” and revealed he became inspired to not leave an inheritance to his children after reading about Warren Buffett ’s thoughts on the topic in a 1986 Fortune article. Alongside Buffett and his former wife Melinda French Gates, the Microsoft co-founder helped establish the Giving Pledge in 2010, a campaign urging the wealthy to give away the majority of their wealth during their lifetime.Warren Buffet has an estimated net worth of $144.6 billion. The 96-year-old Berkshire Hathaway founder has long maintained that his children will not be inheriting his wealth. He famously recommending in 2021, that ultra-wealthy families leave their children "enough so that they can do anything, but not enough that they can do nothing." He declared that his three kids are "going to carve their own place in the world. " Passing down mass amounts of money "just because they came out of the right womb" is an "antisocial act," he said.While Buffett may not be interested in giving his kids an inheritance, he has offered them funds in different ways. In 2006, the billionaire pledged to give all his Berkshire Hathaway shares to charity, including towards several family foundations run by his kids. Earlier this year, he revealed plans to transfer his fortune to a charitable trust upon his death that will be overseen by his children, who must unanimously agree on where to donate the money within a ten-year timeframe.Yvon Chouinard, the founder of the outdoor gear retailer Patagonia once had a net worth of $1.2 billion. In September 2022, he gave up his ten-figure status when he decided to transfer his company to a trust and nonprofit dedicated to environmental causes. The majority of Patagonia is now owned by the nonprofit Holdfast Collective, which will give $100 million annually to combat climate change.However, here the case is a tad bit different. While Chouinard considered leaving his company to his heirs, the children themselves said they didn't want it. Thus, they were left deciding the outcome of their father's vast fortune. “It was important to them that they were not seen as the financial beneficiaries,” Ryan Gellert, CEO of Patagonia, told the New York Times in 2022. “They really embody this notion that every billionaire is a policy failure. ”
Article Summary: An estimated $84 trillion is expected to be passed down in what has been deemed the largest-ever transfer of intergenerational wealth. However, not all billionaires seem to be on board. From Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to Patagonia founder Yvon Chouinard, some have decided against leaving their fortunes to their children.

Article Title: California couple says county entered their property for road-safety work, they spent $300,000 fixing alleged damage and then received a $676,703 bill; fresh federal court order keeps part of fight al
Article Text:
Rubin and Stein said they spent more than $300,000 repairing hazardous conditions they alleged were caused by the county (Representational AI photo)

Six claims against county

Why notice claim was dismissed

Other claims dismissed

Legal fight can continue

A California couple who say Santa Clara County damaged their property while trying to deal with a landslide threatening a public road have been allowed to continue parts of their legal fight. The couple say they spent more than $300,000 repairing the alleged damage, only to later receive a $676,703.22 bill from the county for its work. A federal judge has dismissed their current complaint but allowed them to amend some of their claims.Alejandro V Rubin and Lisa M Stein own property in an area designated as a “high-hazard landslide zone”, according to the court document. Their land includes a hillside overlooking Mount Madonna Road, a public road maintained by Santa Clara County. According to their complaint, a landslide began around March 2024, sending “soil and debris onto Mount Madonna Road”. The situation continued to worsen despite efforts by the couple and the county.In June 2024, the couple told the county that the landslide “posed an imminent threat to public safety”. The county then issued a Summary Abatement Order and entered the property to carry out remediation work. The couple alleged that the work caused substantial damage and “permanently destabilized the hillside”.Rubin and Stein said they spent more than $300,000 repairing hazardous conditions they alleged were caused by the county. They were later sent a $676,703.22 invoice for the county’s mitigation work. They filed their federal lawsuit in March 2026.The lawsuit named Santa Clara County, three county bodies and seven county officials. The couple brought six claims, including alleged violations of procedural due process, a Fifth Amendment taking, failure to train or supervise employees, inverse condemnation, dangerous condition of public property and negligence.The defendants asked the court to dismiss the case. During the proceedings, Rubin and Stein dropped their three state-law claims including inverse condemnation, dangerous condition of public property and negligence. They also sought permission to pursue claims against the named officials individually rather than in their official capacities.The court also removed the County Board of Supervisors, Planning and Building Department and Roads and Airports Department as separate defendants, finding that they were parts of Santa Clara County.The couple alleged that significant excavation work was carried out without “adequate notice or opportunity to appeal”. The county argued that the landslide presented an emergency and allowed officials to act without first holding a hearing.The judge pointed to the couple’s own statement that the landslide posed an imminent threat to public safety. Under California law, counties can take immediate action against a nuisance that poses a threat to public health or safety.The court therefore found that the county could begin the work without giving prior notice. It also said the couple still had an opportunity to seek an administrative hearing with the county.The couple had also alleged that the county's actions amounted to a Fifth Amendment taking by depriving them of the use and enjoyment of their property. During the case, they sought to drop that argument and instead pursue a substantive due-process claim.The judge said the original claim had been presented as a takings claim and could not be changed into a substantive due-process claim at this stage. It was therefore dismissed.The court also dismissed their claim that the county failed to properly train or supervise employees. It found that the complaint did not provide enough facts showing that a county policy, practice or lack of training had caused a constitutional violation.US District Judge Beth Labson Freeman's October 2 order dismissed the current claims but allowed the couple to amend several of them. The court said their lawyer had indicated that additional facts could be provided, meaning amendment would not necessarily be futile.Rubin and Stein can amend their procedural and substantive due-process claims, their failure-to-train or supervise claim and their claims against individual county officials. However, their Fifth Amendment takings allegations and three state-law claims cannot be amended.The couple must file an amended complaint within 45 days of receiving the Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors' final decision after an administrative hearing. The court also said failure to meet the deadline or correct the problems identified in the order would lead to the remaining claims being dismissed with prejudice.
Article Summary: Alejandro V Rubin and Lisa M Stein own property in an area designated as a “high-hazard landslide zone’ Their land includes a hillside overlooking Mount Madonna Road, a public road maintained by Santa Clara County. The couple say they spent more than $300,000 repairing the alleged damage, only to later receive a $676,703.22 bill from the county for its work. A federal judge has dismissed their current complaint but allowed them to amend some of their claims.

Article Title: Florida man arrested after placing virus on woman’s computer, sharing private info in more than 100 TikTok videos
Article Text:
Florida man published more than 100 videos on Tik Tok

Woman alleged a virus was placed on her computer

Investigators also examined alleged location tracking

Police seized electronic devices

Earlier stalking allegations were dropped

Prosecutors revived the computer case

A 36-year-old Florida man was arrested after investigators accused him of gaining unauthorised access to a woman’s computer and posting private information involving women in more than 100 TikTok videos. Mark Stephen Asea of Port St. Lucie was booked into the St Lucie County Jail on September 30 on a felony computer-access charge, with his bond set at $35,000. The case followed an investigation into allegations involving at least two women, including claims that Asea had remotely accessed a computer, obtained passwords and private material, and discussed personal information in his online videos. Investigators also examined claims involving location data, purchases and private conversations. Asea’s earlier stalking allegations were dropped, but prosecutors later revived the computer-related case in September.The investigation centred partly on Asea’s TikTok account, where police say he published more than 100 videos involving one of the women. According to the police affidavit cited by local and national media, some of the videos allegedly contained details about the woman’s personal life and information that investigators believed he should not have had access to.Detectives reviewed videos in which Asea discussed information including a password, phone or device details, purchases and location-related information. The woman told investigators that some of the information had been shared privately and questioned how Asea had obtained it.Asea has presented himself online using descriptions including “grey hat hacker” and “demonologist”. His online profiles have also used terms such as “cybersecurity engineer”, according to reporting based on the police investigation.A separate allegation involved another woman who told investigators that Asea had previously helped her remotely with a computer problem. According to the affidavit, the woman had allowed Asea to access her computer remotely in October 2025 while he helped troubleshoot an application. She later became concerned after allegedly learning that he had installed a programme or virus that could allow continued access without her knowledge or permission.The woman also told police that a photograph from a private conversation later appeared in one of Asea’s TikTok videos. Investigators examined the circumstances surrounding the image and the alleged access to her electronic device. The computer-related allegation ultimately became the focus of the criminal charge filed against Asea in September.Police also investigated allegations that Asea had access to information about a woman’s location. According to the affidavit, detectives reviewed online material in which Asea allegedly discussed GPS information connected to the woman’s phone. The investigation examined whether he had obtained information that would allow him to determine where she was.The case also involved allegations concerning private communications and personal information. Investigators were particularly interested in how information that appeared in Asea’s online content had been obtained and whether it came from devices or accounts that he was not authorised to access.The allegations formed part of a wider investigation into Asea’s interactions with the women and his use of information in his social-media content.The investigation eventually led authorities to search Asea’s residence and collect electronic equipment for examination. According to court documents described in media reports, investigators seized items including computers, mobile phones, external hard drives, USB storage devices, an iPad, a Dell laptop and other networking equipment.Authorities sought to examine the devices for evidence that could establish how information had been obtained or stored. Investigators were interested in material such as passwords, messages, account information, financial records, browser history and location data. The forensic examination was significant because the allegations involved information that investigators believed may have originated from electronic devices or private accounts.Asea's current case follows an earlier criminal investigation. He was initially arrested in April 2026 in connection with allegations that included stalking and unauthorised computer access. However, prosecutors filed a “No Information” in May, meaning the charges then under consideration were not pursued at that stage.A separate civil proceeding also involved a woman seeking protection through a stalking injunction. A temporary order was issued in July, but the case was later dismissed and the injunction was dissolved in September. The criminal investigation nevertheless returned to court later in the year.On September 24, prosecutors reopened the criminal case and filed a new information against Asea. The revived prosecution focuses on a felony allegation involving unauthorised access to a computer or electronic device. Asea was subsequently booked into the St Lucie County Jail on September 30. His bond was set at $35,000.The current case is narrower than the allegations that surrounded the earlier investigation. The stalking allegations that were previously dropped were not simply reinstated as part of the September filing. Instead, the active criminal charge concerns the alleged unauthorised computer access. Asea is due to appear for arraignment on November 19, according to reports citing court records.
Article Summary: Mark Stephen Asea of Port St. Lucie was booked into the St Lucie County Jail on September 30 on a felony computer-access charge. The case followed an investigation into allegations involving at least two women, including claims that Asea had remotely accessed a computer, obtained passwords and private material. Investigators also examined claims involving location data, purchases and private conversations.

Article Title: A ticketing company has sent US$13.8 million in profits to charity instead of shareholders; Hugh Jackman joined Humanitix in 2026 to help expand the model
Article Text:
Representative Image of the Humanitix logo symbolizing charitable contributions through ticket bookings ( AI Generrated Image)

How Humanitix turns booking fees into charitable giving

Where the US$13.8 million has gone

Hugh Jackman's role at Humanitix

Humanitix also reports discounted support for non-profits

A ticketing business built around its profits

A ticket booking fee can help fund more than an event. Humanitix, a not-for-profit ticketing platform, says it has directed US$13.8 million in profits to charitable causes, supporting work in education, healthcare, poverty alleviation and other areas. The company's current 2026 Impact Report puts the detailed total at US$13,822,038. Actor Hugh Jackman joined Humanitix as its Head of Impact in April 2026, several years after the organisation began directing profits to charity. In his own announcement, Jackman said he wanted to “help build” the organisation rather than support it from the sidelines. Humanitix says its model dedicates 100% of the profits from its booking fees to charity, while the fees themselves help cover the costs of running the ticketing platform.Humanitix charges a booking fee on paid tickets sold through its platform. According to its current fee guidance, the fee covers payment-processing and merchant costs when an event uses Humanitix's own payment gateway, as well as the company's staff, servers and other tools used to operate the platform. The company says 100% of the profit generated from those fees is donated. The payment-processing arrangement is not identical for every event.Humanitix says its own payment gateway covers payment-processing costs within the booking fee, while events that use Stripe as their payment gateway incur Stripe's processing fees separately. The company also says booking fees are normally passed on to ticket buyers, although event organisers can choose to absorb them.Humanitix describes itself as a registered charity and not-for-profit organisation. It says it has no shareholders and does not pay dividends to investors. Its 2025 explanation of its donation model says revenue from booking fees is pooled with operating costs to determine how much can be donated to partner charities. That means the amount generated by an individual event cannot simply be equated with a fixed portion of its booking fees.Humanitix's 2026 Impact Report provides a breakdown of the profits it says it has distributed. Poverty alleviation accounts for 39.74%, or US$5,492,240.57, while education accounts for 36.97%, or US$5,109,863.55. Healthcare represents 17.18%, or US$2,375,092.19. A further 4.2%, or US$580,708.13, is listed under support for Indigenous groups. The remaining 1.91%, or US$264,133.56, is categorised as other giving, including environmental and human-rights causes. The figures are published directly in Humanitix's 2026 Impact Report.The report lists a broader set of areas supported through Humanitix's charitable programme, including food security, safety and dignity, the environment, children and youth services and what the company calls life's basic necessities. Its listed charity partners include The Life You Can Save, GiveDirectly, Room to Read, Educate Girls, Food 4 Education, Healthy Learners and other organisations working in education, healthcare and poverty alleviation. Humanitix's descriptions of individual partners give examples of the work supported. Food 4 Education, for example, provides school meals in Kenya, while Healthy Learners works with the Zambian government on school-based healthcare. Educate Girls works in rural India to support girls' education, and Room to Read focuses on literacy and girls' education in low-income communities. These descriptions come from Humanitix's own partner listings rather than independent assessments of the organisations' overall effectiveness.In a letter dated April 21, 2026, Jackman announced his appointment as Humanitix's Head of Impact. In his letter published by Humanitix, he explained that the more he learned about the organisation, the more he wanted to become involved in building it. Jackman also described Humanitix's model as different from a conventional company that makes money and later donates a portion to charity. He wrote that the organisation directs its profits towards its mission and said the model was the reason he wanted to take an active role.At the time of his appointment, Jackman wrote that Humanitix had collectively directed more than A$20 million towards projects addressing global poverty and education. Humanitix's current Australian-facing pages display a more precise Australian-dollar figure of A$20,796,400, while the US impact materials give the detailed total as US$13,822,038. The figures are different currency expressions of the reported donation total, not separate amounts that should be added together. Jackman's appointment therefore came after the organisation had already accumulated most of the reported giving. His stated role is to help build Humanitix's impact as the organisation continues its work.The company's charitable model extends beyond direct donations. Humanitix offers eligible charities, schools and other non-profit organisations a discounted booking-fee rate. Its 2026 Impact Report says eligible organisations have used the discounted rate to run more than 300,000 events. The US version of the report puts the value of these discounted services at US$10.33 million and describes them as in-kind donations. Because Humanitix publishes different currency figures on different regional versions of its site, this article uses the US report's figure rather than attempting to convert or reconcile the regional amounts independently.The report also says Humanitix employees received a portion of the company's profit pool over the past 3 years and were able to direct those funds to charities of their choice. Humanitix puts the total of these staff-directed donations at US$991,853. The report does not separately state whether that amount is included within or additional to the US$13.8 million headline donation figure, so the two figures should not be combined.Humanitix's model is ultimately based on using a commercial ticketing service to generate profits for charitable giving. The company says its booking fees contribute towards operating the platform, while all profit generated from those fees is directed towards its charitable mission. Its current impact report says more than US$13.8 million has been donated to charity and identifies education, poverty alleviation and healthcare as its largest reported areas of giving. The report also identifies food security, environmental protection, support for Indigenous groups, safety and dignity, and children's services among the causes it supports.Jackman joined the organisation in 2026 with the stated aim of helping build that model. His appointment came after years of charitable giving by Humanitix, meaning the US$13.8 million figure reflects the organisation's accumulated impact rather than donations generated during Jackman's tenure. For ticket buyers, the company's proposition is straightforward: the booking fee attached to an event can contribute to a business whose profits are directed towards charitable causes rather than shareholders.
Article Summary: Humanitix charges a booking fee on paid tickets sold through its platform. The company says 100% of the profit generated from those fees is donated. Actor Hugh Jackman joined Humanitix as its Head of Impact in April 2026. In his own announcement, Jackman said he wanted to ‘help build’ the organisation.

Article Title: 650 drones overnight: Ukraine unleashes massive strike on Moscow region
Article Text:
Moscow under drone swarm: Ukraine launches massive overnight attack

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you support international intervention in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia? Yes, definitely No, it's better to let them resolve it themselves 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Ukraine launched an overnight drone attack involving around 650 drones targeting the Moscow region, Russian authorities said on Tuesday, in one of the largest such attacks on the Russian capital and its surroundings in the past two years.Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 105 drones were downed near the city. Regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said a 20-year-old man was killed in a village on the outskirts of Moscow and several homes were damaged. RIA Novosti reported that six people were wounded.This comes as Ukraine’s Defence Ministry on Monday claimed that more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity had been put out of action by its armed forces. “More than 51 per cent of Russia’s oil refining capacity is out of action”, the ministry said on X.The ministry said recent attacks had targeted refineries and processing facilities in Moscow, Yaroslavl, KINEF (Kirishi), Ust-Luga, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov and Syzran, among other locations.Ukraine has been targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure in an effort to curb Moscow’s revenue that funds its war efforts. Ukraine’s Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara said the partial disruption was the result of “carefully planned and systematic work” to destroy Moscow’s military-economic potential.Russia has said it plans to step up strikes on infrastructure targets, including in Kyiv, as winter approaches.
Article Summary: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 105 drones were downed near the city. A 20-year-old man was killed in a village on the outskirts of Moscow and several homes were damaged. This comes as Ukraine’s Defence Ministry on Monday claimed that more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity had been put out of action by its armed forces.

Article Title: From 1946, NSW planted South African bitou bush to stabilise coastal sand dunes; decades later it had spread along 46% of the state's coastline and threatened native ecosystems
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A plant brought in to stabilise dunes

How bitou bush spread

Native plants and animals face pressure

Efforts now focus on containment and restoration

A plant introduced with a practical purpose along the New South Wales (NSW) coast eventually became a major environmental weed. South African bitou bush was deliberately planted along the NSW coastline between 1946 and 1968 to help stabilise sand dunes, according to the NSW Environment and Heritage department. The fast-growing shrub later spread rapidly and is now found along 46% of the state's coastline, with some infestations extending up to 10 kilometres inland. What was once used to control shifting sand has since become a threat to native coastal vegetation and wildlife, prompting long-running efforts to contain and remove it.Bitou bush, scientifically known as Chrysanthemoides monilifera subsp. rotundata, is native to South Africa. NSW Environment and Heritage says it is thought to have initially reached Australia in ship ballast before later being deliberately used for dune stabilisation. Its deliberate planting along the NSW coast began in 1946 and continued through 1968. The plant was valued because it grew quickly and could help hold loose coastal sand in place. Historical government documents also record its use to stabilise and revegetate dunes affected by coastal sand mining.Planting took place at a number of coastal locations, including Ballina, Byron Bay, Crescent Head, Iluka, Lake Munmorah, Port Macquarie, Redhead, The Entrance and Tweed Heads. The same characteristics that made bitou bush useful for stabilisation, however, also helped it become difficult to control once it established beyond planted areas.Once established along the coastline, bitou bush spread through a combination of deliberate planting and natural expansion. The NSW government now records it along 46% of the state's coastline, with the north coast particularly heavily affected. In some locations, the shrub has moved as far as 10 kilometres inland. Bitou bush is capable of growing rapidly and forming dense stands. Rather than simply occupying empty spaces, it can move into existing coastal plant communities and create thick shrub layers.That expansion has changed the character of some dunes, headlands and other coastal habitats. Earlier government assessments described an even wider distribution at different points in time, reflecting differences in surveys, definitions and assessment periods. A NSW Scientific Committee determination in 1999, for example, reported the weed on 90% of the state's sandy coast. The current NSW Environment and Heritage data shows the figure as 46% of the state's coastline.The main environmental concern is not simply the presence of an introduced shrub but what happens when it becomes dominant. According to NSW Environment and Heritage, bitou bush invades coastal heathlands, grasslands, woodlands and forests. It can form dense stands that replace native plants and alter habitats used by native animals. Infestations can also smother vegetation communities found on sand dunes and headlands.The NSW Bitou Threat Abatement Plan identified 157 native plant species, three plant populations and 24 ecological communities as being at risk from bitou bush and boneseed invasion. The plan also identified 24 native animal species potentially threatened by the spread of the weeds. Because of these impacts, the NSW Scientific Committee has listed the invasion of native plant communities by bitou bush and boneseed as a key threatening process affecting native plants and animals.Managing the weed is now a long-term conservation task. Bitou bush and the related South African plant boneseed were collectively listed as Weeds of National Significance in 2000. NSW has also developed a Threat Abatement Plan that directs control towards sites where removing the weed can provide the greatest benefit to threatened species and ecological communities.The approach involves more than simply removing individual plants. Control programmes involve government agencies, local authorities, community groups, Aboriginal groups, land managers and bush regenerators. The NSW plan identifies 169 priority sites, alongside northern and southern containment zones intended to limit further spread and protect important native vegetation.Under the NSW Biosecurity Act 2015, specific requirements also apply to bitou bush management. In areas north of Cape Byron and south of Point Perpendicular, eradication is required, while the central coastal distribution is managed through containment measures.The history of bitou bush shows how a species introduced to solve one environmental problem can create another when it spreads beyond its intended role. Decades after it was planted to stabilise NSW sand dunes, the shrub has become widespread enough to require coordinated control, with restoration efforts now aimed at giving native coastal ecosystems space to recover. The continuing challenge is to prevent further spread while gradually restoring the native vegetation and habitats that have been affected by the invasive plant, a process that is likely to require sustained monitoring and management for years to come.
Article Summary: South African bitou bush was deliberately planted along the NSW coastline between 1946 and 1968. The fast-growing shrub later spread rapidly and is now found along 46% of the state's coastline. In some locations, the shrub has moved as far as 10 kilometres inland. Infestations can smother vegetation communities found on sand dunes and headlands.

Article Title: How flydubai security failure, across 3 countries, almost led to 'Israel’s 9/11’
Article Text:
File photo: A flydubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport

Oman flagged him, but the warning did not travel

Hammam al-Hammami

Israel had his name, and still let him fly

The cockpit attack

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for improving airline security? Cross-Border Intelligence Sharing Stronger Background Checks for Crew Better Security Checks at Airports Stronger Cockpit Security & Access Control 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A string of security failures across Oman, the UAE and Israel allowed the flydubai co-pilot to get into the cockpit, a Wall Street Journal investigation has found. The lapses nearly led to an aviation disaster reminiscent of 9/11, despite authorities having reasons to be concerned about him.The failures began in Oman, where authorities had scrutinised Hamam al-Hammami’s online activity and found he showed too much interest in radical ideology to be trusted as a pilot at state carrier Oman Air. They banned him from flying, sent him to a deradicalisation programme and moved him to a desk job, but did not broadly communicate their concerns about him.When al-Hammami joined flydubai in February, the airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience, the WSJ reported. It conducted a criminal-background check, but the earlier concerns that had led Oman to remove him from flying were not passed on to the new employer. The operator, flydubai, later assigned him to the sensitive Tel Aviv route, which he flew multiple times.Oman’s handling of the case also created another missed opportunity. People familiar with the matter said that had the country formally withdrawn al-Hammami’s pilot licence over its concerns, the action would likely have been flagged to the UAE.Instead, the concerns about his extremism were not communicated more widely.The final layer of failures came in Israel, where foreign airlines are required to submit passenger and crew lists before arriving.Airline operator flydubai had submitted the manifest for Flight 1073, but Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews. The ministry also said it had never asked to access a database created in 2023 to help authorised agencies review passenger and crew information because it did not know the database was operational or that it could use it.There was an even more basic warning that should have stopped al-Hammami from flying to Israel. Pilots from countries such as Oman, which does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, are barred from flying to the country. Yet al-Hammami was allowed onto the Tel Aviv-bound flight.Israel’s own previous warnings also raise questions about how the system failed. A classified May 2024 report by the country’s comptroller general had warned that aviation security had grown lax, with fragmented responsibilities and unclear lines of authority. The report also identified manpower and budget problems affecting oversight by the transportation ministry.The security failures culminated halfway through Flight 1073, when al-Hammami attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe after excusing himself to pray.The wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to enter and overpower the co-pilot. They then helped pull the aircraft out of a dangerous dive.The UAE’s attorney general has described the incident as an attempted terrorist act. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel suspect al-Hammami was trying to crash the aircraft in Tel Aviv, according to people familiar with their thinking. All three countries are investigating whether he acted alone; so far, investigators have not found links to a foreign power or major terrorist organisation, those people said.The incident has since prompted Israel to review the security of foreign airline flights to the country.
Article Summary: Oman Air banned Hamam al-Hammami from flying, but did not communicate concerns about him to flydubai. The airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience. Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews.

Article Title: Russia plague scare puts US on watch as Rubio flags possible internal spread
Article Text:
US monitors suspected plague case in Russian lab worker amid fears of internal spread, says Rubio

The United States is closely monitoring a suspected plague infection involving a laboratory worker in Russia amid concerns that the disease may have spread internally, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said, while stressing that Washington's information on the case is based on details provided by Russian officials.Rubio made the remarks while speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a European visit. He said the US was aware of the case through information provided by Russian officials and was closely watching the situation over concerns that the infection could have spread internally.Rubio said the information available to Washington indicated that a worker at a Russian laboratory had been infected and that there was concern the infection may have spread within the facility.“We don't - we know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided, which is it seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that could have spread, at least internally,” he said.Rubio also indicated that quarantine measures had been taken in connection with the incident, although he did not provide details about the number of people affected or whether any internal transmission had been confirmed.He noted that travel between the US and Russia was currently limited, but said an infection that escapes its initial setting could spread quickly. “There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously. But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” he said.The remarks came after a laboratory worker at Russia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died following pneumonia of unknown origin, prompting quarantine and medical monitoring of her contacts. Russian authorities have not confirmed plague as the cause of death, although reports have raised the possibility of pneumonic plague.Reports also alleged that the worker may have been exposed to plague bacteria in a laboratory incident, but Russian authorities have denied evidence of an accident involving dangerous pathogens. Authorities have identified the known contacts and reported no new cases among institute staff.There is also no confirmation that the worker had pneumonic plague or that human-to-human transmission occurred.
Article Summary: US monitoring suspected plague case in Russian lab worker amid fears of internal spread, says Rubio. US secretary of state says Washington's information on the case is based on details provided by Russian officials. A laboratory worker at Russia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died following pneumonia.

Article Title: Kristin Davis helped rescue one-year-old elephant after finding her alone in Kenya; years later, Chaimu returned to the wild and inspired a sculpture
Article Text:
Sheldrick Wildlife Trust

Kristin Davis helps rescue an abandoned elephant calf in Kenya

From the nursery to Tsavo East: Chaimu learns life among wild elephants

PC: Sheldrick Wildlife Trust

A 2011 Kenya visit strengthens Davis’s ties to elephant conservation

A longer commitment to wildlife conservation

Chaimu becomes part of a larger conservation project

From an orphaned calf to life in the wild

In 2009, a holiday in Kenya brought actress Kristin Davis into an unexpected encounter with an abandoned elephant calf. While staying in the Chyulu Hills, Davis and staff from Kampi Ya Kanzi came across the young elephant on its own. When the calf was still without its mother several days later, a decision was made to intervene. The orphan, later named Chaimu, was about a year old and was taken into the care of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, now known as the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Sixteen years on, Chaimu has become part of a very different story. After years of rehabilitation and time learning alongside wild elephants, she has returned to the wild, marking the latest stage in a long journey from a vulnerable orphan to a fully independent elephant living among her own kind once again.Davis was holidaying in the Chyulu Hills when she and people working at Kampi Ya Kanzi spotted the calf. At first, there was uncertainty over whether the elephant had simply become separated from its herd. But the situation did not change over the following days.With the calf continuing to remain alone, the group decided that intervention was necessary. The DSWT was contacted and arrangements were made to rescue the young elephant.She was named Chaimu and, at roughly one year old, began a rehabilitation process that would eventually take her from the Nairobi Nursery to the organisation’s reintegration programme in Tsavo East.Chaimu’s care did not end with her arrival at the Nairobi Nursery. Orphaned elephants in rehabilitation need to develop many of the behaviours they would ordinarily learn from their families, including how to interact with other elephants and function within a herd.After graduating from the nursery, Chaimu moved to the Ithumba Reintegration Centre in Tsavo East. The centre allows older orphan elephants to spend increasing amounts of time around wild elephants before making the transition away from human care.That process was reflected in Davis’s later descriptions of Chaimu. The elephant was regularly mixing with wild herds and learning the skills needed for life outside the sanctuary system.The encounter did not become an isolated episode in Davis’s life. She continued supporting the organisation and used her public profile to draw attention to its work with orphaned elephants and wider conservation issues.Her involvement included visits to Kenya. In July 2011, she returned with her friend Ame and filmmaker Roz Edwards, spending time at the Nairobi Nursery before travelling to Ithumba in Tsavo East. During that visit, she stayed at Ithumba Camp, which had been established alongside the reintegration centre and was intended to support limited responsible tourism in the northern part of Tsavo East.Davis also spoke publicly about Chaimu and the charity’s work, including an appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show. She has continued to identify elephant conservation and the illegal ivory trade among the issues she has highlighted.Davis’s work with elephants has since extended beyond her connection with Chaimu. She also served as a Goodwill Ambassador for UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, in 2017, according to The UN Refugee Agency.Her interest in conservation has also crossed into film. The Perfect World Foundation Award says that in 2014, she executive produced and financed Gardeners of Eden, a documentary about the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust and its efforts to protect elephants. The film received recognition at several film festivals, including the Elephant Hero Award at the UN-sponsored International Elephant Film Festival in 2016, and was later a finalist for a Peabody Award.In September 2023, Davis received The Perfect World Foundation Award for her contribution to raising awareness around wildlife and biodiversity conservation.Years after the original rescue, Chaimu’s story became connected to The Great Elephant Migration, a conservation art project involving a travelling collection of elephant sculptures. Davis has supported the project and said she wanted to help raise awareness and funds for conservation work.A sculpture representing Chaimu is part of the migrating herd. Its inclusion links the animal Davis encountered as an orphaned calf in Kenya with the elephant she later saw progressing through rehabilitation and towards life in the wild.By then, Chaimu was 16 years old and had been reintegrated into the wild. Her story therefore spans much more than the original rescue. It covers the long period between being found alone in the Chyulu Hills and eventually becoming capable of living beyond the protection of the rehabilitation programme.Chaimu’s journey illustrates the lengthy nature of elephant rehabilitation. The rescue itself happened quickly once it became clear that the calf was not being reunited with her herd, but the process that followed took years.From the Nairobi Nursery to Ithumba, Chaimu gradually spent more time in an environment where wild elephants could provide experiences and social interactions that a young orphan would otherwise have gained from its family. Her eventual return to the wild marked the later stage of that process.For Davis, the connection began with an encounter during a Kenyan holiday in 2009. More than a decade later, Chaimu’s name remains attached to her conservation work, this time through a sculpture travelling with The Great Elephant Migration and representing an elephant that survived the loss of its original herd and went on to rejoin wild elephants.
Article Summary: Kristin Davis came across an abandoned elephant calf in Kenya in 2009. The calf, later named Chaimu, was taken into the care of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Davis continued supporting the organisation and used her public profile to draw attention to its work with orphaned elephants and wider conservation issues.

Article Title: In 2016, an Arkansas woman put one wooden pantry outside a church with food and toiletries; within three months the idea had gone global, and the movement now maps 2,301 mini pantries
Article Text:
The idea soon travelled beyond Fayetteville and Arkansas, developing into networks of mini pantries in communities across the United States and elsewhere. Some local networks began maintaining their own maps, including the Lowcountry Blessing Box Project and Pātaka Kai Open Street Pantries.

From books to basic needs

A community takes ownership

A small idea spreads

The power of something small

Sometimes an idea for helping people does not begin with a foundation, a fundraiser or a grand plan. Sometimes it starts with a small wooden box, a few cans of food and the simple realisation that a neighbourhood can look after its own. In Fayetteville, Arkansas, Jessica McClard was fascinated by the Little Free Library movement, which was bringing tiny book-sharing structures into neighbourhoods. She began wondering whether the same principle could be applied to something more immediate than books. What if people could share food, toiletries and everyday essentials in exactly the same way?In May 2016, that question became the Little Free Pantry and that slowly became a huge success. Scroll down to read this success story.According to ABC News, McClard installed what she believed to be the first Little Free Pantry outside Good Shepherd Lutheran Church in Fayetteville. The small wooden structure was stocked with canned food, personal-care products, paper goods and other necessities. The model was deliberately uncomplicated. People who had something to spare could leave it. Anyone who needed something could take it.There were no forms, membership cards or complicated systems to navigate.The pantry quickly demonstrated how much demand existed for such a simple resource. Items that disappeared particularly quickly included deodorant, toothpaste, toothbrushes, diapers, feminine hygiene products, toilet paper and paper towels. Food remained important, but the experiment also highlighted how expensive everyday necessities can become when household budgets are stretched.What made the pantry distinctive was not simply what was placed inside it, but what happened around it. As per the same report, people began adding school supplies for children and other useful items. The structure itself became something of a community canvas, with neighbours decorating it for occasions such as Memorial Day. The pantry was no longer just McClard's project. It had begun to belong to the neighbourhood. Handwritten thank-you notes left inside the pantry became another small but meaningful sign of its impact. The reach also extended beyond the immediate area, with people travelling from other places to visit the original pantry.The idea soon travelled beyond Fayetteville and Arkansas, developing into networks of mini pantries in communities across the United States and elsewhere. Some local networks began maintaining their own maps, including the Lowcountry Blessing Box Project and Pātaka Kai Open Street Pantries, adds the official website of Little Free Pantry. The wider movement now maps 2,301 mini pantries, illustrating how a hyper-local experiment can develop into a much broader community-driven network, the website adds.The project has also found connections with wider cultural and charitable initiatives. In 2021, the Little Free Pantry partnered with Celadon Books and the Jane Goodall Institute around the launch of Jane Goodall's The Book of Hope, bringing the idea of everyday community action into a broader conversation about hope and collective responsibility.The lasting appeal of the Little Free Pantry lies partly in its simplicity. It does not attempt to solve food insecurity through a sweeping programme. Instead, it creates a visible point where one person can help another without ceremony. Its success also reveals something easily overlooked about community support: people do not always need to be told how to help. Sometimes they simply need a place to put their generosity.Image Courtesy: The Chronicle of Philanthropy
Article Summary: Jessica McClard installed the first Little Free Pantry outside a church in Fayetteville, Arkansas, in May 2016. The small wooden structure was stocked with canned food, personal-care products, paper goods and other necessities. The model was deliberately uncomplicated. People who had something to spare could leave it.

Article Title: Wyoming Army veteran fought a mountain lion bare-handed for 20 seconds to save his dog; said cat ‘put me right down’
Article Text:
Image: Cowboy State Daily

How a Wyoming Army veteran 's trip to photograph elk turned into a fight

The kick that made the mountain lion turn on him

Diesel escaped without serious injury

Wyoming Game and Fish investigated the encounter

What to do if a mountain lion appears

An Army veteran from Cody, Wyoming, found himself in a fight with a juvenile mountain lion after the predator attacked his two-year-old Labrador retriever, Diesel, near the South Fork Road area outside Cody. Adam Borkhus had driven into the area hoping to photograph elk and was carrying bear spray and a pistol when he heard his dog yelp. He ran towards the sound and found the mountain lion on top of Diesel. Because the animals were entangled, Borkhus feared shooting could hit his dog, so he kicked the mountain lion. The animal immediately turned on him, knocked him to the ground and fought with him for roughly 20 seconds before fleeing. Borkhus suffered scratches, while Diesel escaped without significant injuries.Borkhus had travelled with Diesel to the South Fork area near Cody, where he hoped to photograph elk. KTVQ reported that rainy weather had made him think the conditions could produce interesting photographs. He stopped near the Deer Creek Trailhead and let Diesel out of the vehicle. The situation changed within moments. Borkhus heard Diesel yelp and went to investigate, discovering a young mountain lion on top of his dog.The encounter occurred in heavy cover along South Fork Road, according to Wyoming Game and Fish officials.Borkhus already had two forms of protection with him. He was carrying bear spray and a pistol because of the presence of grizzlies in the area. However, the close-range struggle between Diesel and the mountain lion created another problem: either weapon could potentially injure his own dog.“There wasn’t time to think,” Borkhus told Cowboy State Daily, explaining that his immediate concern was protecting Diesel.With Diesel underneath the mountain lion, Borkhus decided to intervene physically. He kicked the animal, which caused it to turn away from the Labrador and towards him.The mountain lion then pounced on Borkhus and struck him in the chest, knocking him onto his back. The Wyoming man said he tried to keep the animal's mouth away from his neck and face while using his other hand to fight it. Borkhus estimated that the physical struggle lasted around 20 seconds, although KTVQ reported that he described the entire encounter as lasting less than 30 seconds. During the fight, he attempted to punch the mountain lion as it repeatedly swiped at him.Despite being much larger than the animal, Borkhus said he was surprised by its strength. He described himself as 6 feet 3 inches tall and 320 pounds and estimated that the juvenile mountain lion weighed no more than about 70 pounds.“He hit me in the chest and put me right down. That thing was strong,” Borkhus told Cowboy State Daily. The mountain lion eventually broke away and disappeared into the surrounding vegetation.Once the mountain lion fled, Borkhus discovered that Diesel had escaped the confrontation without significant injuries. The Labrador apparently had little interest in continuing the adventure. According to Borkhus, Diesel ran directly back to the vehicle and waited there while his owner recovered from the encounter. Borkhus later joked about his dog's reaction, saying Diesel appeared to be communicating that they should leave. He also said the experience did not seem to change the dog's personality. “Nope. He’s just his own dumb self,” Borkhus told Cowboy State Daily when asked whether Diesel had become nervous or behaved differently afterwards.Borkhus, meanwhile, was left with scratches on his face, hands and arms. KTVQ reported that the injuries were not severe enough to require stitches. The encounter nevertheless resulted in medical treatment. Borkhus received a tetanus booster and antibiotics, and doctors also began a precautionary course of rabies vaccinations.Borkhus contacted the Wyoming Game and Fish Department after the incident. Wildlife personnel responded that evening and searched the area for the mountain lion, but they were unable to locate it.Officials confirmed that a dog had been attacked in heavy cover along South Fork Road near the Deer Creek Trailhead, followed by an attack on a person. Based on their investigation, the department said the incident was most likely a surprise encounter that triggered aggressive defensive behaviour from the mountain lion. The department said it would continue monitoring the area.That assessment is significant because it distinguishes the incident from a mountain lion deliberately pursuing a person. Wyoming Game and Fish describes mountain lions as the state's most elusive large carnivore and says they are rarely seen.The department explains that their cryptic behaviour is linked to their successful stalking and ambush hunting strategy. Deer and elk are their primary food sources in Wyoming, although research has documented mountain lions eating other mammals, including porcupines, raccoons, beavers and coyotes.The animal involved in Borkhus's encounter was described as a juvenile. A representative of the Mountain Lion Foundation told Cowboy State Daily that a mountain lion of that size could potentially still be associated with its mother, since young lions generally remain with their mothers until around the age of two.Wyoming Game and Fish says conflicts between people and mountain lions are rare, but it provides specific advice for people travelling in lion habitat.The department recommends avoiding solitary recreation when possible because groups are more likely to make enough noise to prevent a surprise encounter. People should never approach a mountain lion and should give the animal a route to escape.If someone encounters a mountain lion, the department advises remaining calm and speaking in a calm, firm manner. The animal should not be chased or cornered.Most importantly, Wyoming Game and Fish says that if a mountain lion attacks, people should fight back and defend themselves. The department also asks people to report mountain lion sightings and encounters to wildlife authorities.The brief fight began with Borkhus trying to save his dog and ended with both the man and the Labrador making it back to their vehicle. Despite the frightening encounter, Borkhus indicated that he and Diesel planned to continue enjoying the outdoors together.
Article Summary: Adam Borkhus heard his dog yelp and found a mountain lion on top of him. He kicked the animal, which caused it to turn on him and attack him. The two-year- old Labrador retriever escaped without serious injury. Wyoming Game and Fish officials said the incident was most likely a surprise.

Article Title: Meet Kimberley Christopher, the Florida State doctoral candidate who developed a plasma process designed to destroy PFAS; after winning a collegiate pitch competition, she's now testing the tech throu
Article Text:
Why PFAS are difficult to destroy

From capturing PFAS to breaking them down

30 interviews helped shape the idea

From pitch competition to NSF I-Corps

100 interviews in seven weeks

A Florida State University doctoral candidate is trying to tackle one of the most persistent classes of environmental contaminants with a technology designed not just to capture PFAS, but potentially destroy them. Kimberley Christopher, a doctoral candidate in Florida State University’s Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, has developed a patent-pending plasma process that uses electrons to trigger the breakdown of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, better known as PFAS or “forever chemicals.” After winning a collegiate startup pitch competition, Christopher is now testing the technology’s commercial potential through the National Science Foundation’s I-Corps program.The NSF-backed project, led by FSU chemical engineering professor Bruce R. Locke, is examining whether the technology can become a cost-competitive, energy-efficient way of destroying PFAS in water. The active I-Corps award runs from September 2026 through August 2027 and provides $50,000 in funding for the team to assess its translation and commercial potential.PFAS refers to a large class of human-made chemicals that have been used for decades because of their resistance to heat, water, oil and grease.They have been used in products ranging from nonstick cookware and stain-resistant materials to firefighting foams and some industrial applications. Their chemical stability, however, also makes many PFAS extremely difficult to break down once they enter the environment.US health authorities say 97% of people in US have measurable PFAS in their blood, while exposure can occur through contaminated drinking water, food, consumer products and contaminated sites. The US Environmental Protection Agency has also established drinking-water limits for several PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, reflecting concerns over their potential health effects.The challenge is not simply removing the chemicals from water. Some existing treatment approaches concentrate PFAS and transfer them into another material, leaving the contaminated substance to be managed or disposed of later. That is where Christopher's research takes a different approach.Christopher is working with Locke, FSU engineering innovation director Robert Wandell and chemistry professor Igor Alabugin on an electron-based framework for PFAS destruction.The approach uses nonthermal plasma and electrons to initiate chemical reactions that weaken the carbon-fluorine bonds characteristic of PFAS. According to the NSF project description, an electron injected into a PFAS molecule can trigger carbon-fluorine bond fragmentation, with the electron subsequently regenerated. The proposed mechanism therefore allows the electron to act catalytically rather than simply being consumed in the reaction.Research presented by Christopher and her FSU collaborators has focused on electron upconversion, a process intended to generate stronger reducing agents from relatively mild electron donors. Their computational work suggests that the approach can weaken carbon-fluorine bonds and promote degradation of certain PFAS compounds in nonthermal plasma systems.FSU called the resulting technology the Radi-Reactor plasma process. The university said it is designed to permanently destroy PFAS rather than merely transfer the contaminants from water into another waste stream. The distinction is important because Christopher's work is still in the research and commercialisation-validation stage. The technology is being evaluated through I-Corps to determine where it could work best and which customers would actually need it.Christopher did not initially enter her doctoral program intending to become an entrepreneur. Her research is in computational physical organic chemistry, but a regional I-Corps program introduced her to the commercial side of scientific research.As part of the regional program, Christopher conducted 30 discovery interviews with potential users and stakeholders. The goal was to understand how organisations currently deal with PFAS contamination, what problems remain unresolved and which potential customer groups could benefit most from a destruction technology.PFAS contamination affects a wide range of industries and waste streams, making the customer-discovery process particularly important. The NSF project identifies possible applications including PFAS-rich landfill leachate, firefighting-foam waste, industrial wastewater and drinking water. Christopher's experience eventually took the technology from laboratory discussions to a competitive pitch.After completing the regional I-Corps program, Christopher was nominated by FSU's Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship to participate in the Florida Venture Forum Collegiate Pitch Competition. There, she presented the PFAS technology to investors, venture capitalists and other potential supporters. With support from FSU's IGNITE program, Christopher won first place, according to the university.The win helped move the project into the next phase. Christopher's team began the NSF's national I-Corps program in early September 2026. Unlike a conventional scientific research grant, I-Corps focuses heavily on customer discovery and determining whether a laboratory invention can become a viable product or business.The NSF describes I-Corps as a seven-week entrepreneurial training program designed to help scientists and engineers move promising inventions beyond the laboratory and toward commercialisation. Since its launch in 2012, more than 2,500 teams have participated, with nearly 1,400 subsequently launching startups, according to the NSF.The next stage is considerably larger than Christopher's first round of customer research. Her team plans to complete 100 discovery interviews over seven weeks, from September through October, as it investigates potential markets and identifies the customer segment most likely to benefit from the technology.The goal is not simply to prove that the chemistry works. Christopher also wants to determine where the process could have the greatest real-world impact and whether it can eventually compete on cost and efficiency with existing approaches. That distinction is central to the I-Corps process. The NSF says the program is designed to reduce the risks involved in moving technologies from laboratories into the marketplace by forcing researchers to test assumptions with potential customers and industry participants.Christopher hopes the work will eventually form the basis of a new company called Radical Solutions Corp. Her longer-term goal is to make the PFAS-destruction technology more effective and cost-competitive while finding applications where permanent destruction offers a clear advantage over simply concentrating or transferring the contaminants.For now, the FSU researcher is still at the crucial testing stage. The technology has not yet become a commercial PFAS treatment system, and its performance, economics and scalability remain subjects of ongoing evaluation.But the path from a doctoral research project to a statewide pitch competition and now a federally funded I-Corps program illustrates how university research can move toward the marketplace.For Christopher, the next test is no longer confined to the laboratory. It is whether a technology designed to break apart some of the most persistent chemicals in the environment can also solve a practical problem for the industries and communities dealing with them.
Article Summary: Florida State University doctoral candidate Kimberley Christopher has developed a plasma process that uses electrons to trigger the breakdown of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, better known as PFAS or “forever chemicals” After winning a collegiate startup pitch competition, Christopher is now testing the technology's commercial potential through the National Science Foundation’s I-Corps program.

Article Title: Meet Nick Grewal who received the Entrepreneur of the Year Award; he founded Nashoba Networks, acquired by Cisco in 1996, before building ePropelled, a global propulsion company
Article Text:
Nashoba Networks and the Cisco deal

From technology investor to another startup

Why Grewal received the award

More than three decades after entering the technology industry, entrepreneur Nick Grewal has added another distinction to his career: the 2026 Entrepreneur of the Year Award from the New Hampshire Tech Alliance, according to a press release by Access Newswire.Grewal, founder, chairman and chief executive officer of ePropelled, was named the recipient of the award in September and formally received it at the Tech Alliance’s Innovation Summit in Nashua on October 6. The recognition follows a career spanning networking technology, investments in high-tech companies, and, more recently, electric propulsion systems for uncrewed vehicles.The New Hampshire Tech Alliance said Grewal has spent more than four decades building companies and advancing emerging technologies. Before turning his attention to autonomous systems, he founded Nashoba Networks, a company that Cisco acquired in 1996.
