He later founded ePropelled in 2018, taking his career from computer networking into a field focused on electrification, propulsion and autonomous vehicles.One of the biggest milestones in Grewal's earlier career came in the 1990s, when he founded Nashoba Networks, a Massachusetts technology company working on Token Ring switching.Cisco's own acquisition records confirm that the company announced an agreement to acquire Nashoba Networks on August 6, 1996. Cisco described Nashoba as a privately held company focused on Token Ring switching technologies and said the acquisition would expand its offerings for high-performance switched workgroup and backbone Token Ring networks.The deal was completed the following month. In a September 19, 1996 announcement, Cisco said it had completed its purchase of Nashoba Networks and that the transaction followed an August stock-swap agreement. According to Cisco, shares worth approximately $100 million were to be exchanged for all outstanding Nashoba shares and options.Grewal subsequently served as a Cisco vice president, according to his profile published by Smart Business Dealmakers. The Nashoba chapter was only one part of a broader technology career. Before and around that period, Grewal held senior executive positions at companies including Proteon and CrossComm, both of which became publicly traded during his tenure, according to the New Hampshire Tech Alliance.After the Cisco acquisition, Grewal continued working in technology and investment. Between 1998 and 2018, he invested in and advised more than 40 companies, many of them based in New Hampshire, according to the Tech Alliance. His next major entrepreneurial chapter began in 2018, when he founded ePropelled.The company's original focus was electric vehicle propulsion, with a broader goal of developing highly efficient electrical power, propulsion and energy-management systems. ePropelled says it was founded in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 2018, with Grewal providing the initial private investment.Grewal has led the company as CEO since May 2018, according to ePropelled's leadership profile. The company now develops electric propulsion and energy-management technologies for air, land and water applications, with a particular focus on uncrewed systems.Unlike Nashoba Networks, which operated in the networking technology sector, ePropelled is focused on the growing intersection of electrification and autonomous systems. The New Hampshire Tech Alliance describes the company as designing and manufacturing intelligent propulsion and energy-management systems for uncrewed vehicles operating across air, land and sea. Its technologies are aimed at applications where propulsion efficiency, energy use and system control can affect the performance and endurance of autonomous platforms.The company has expanded beyond its original US base. ePropelled currently has operations, engineering and production facilities in the US, UK and India, according to its investor-relations information. Its UK operations grew after ePropelled acquired ElectronicaUK Ltd in 2018, while its Coventry facility opened in 2022.In 2023, ePropelled moved its headquarters from Massachusetts to Laconia, New Hampshire. The company says it now has more than 40 global customers and develops propulsion products for uncrewed aerial, ground and marine platforms, alongside industrial and other electric-motor applications.The Entrepreneur of the Year award is not new. The New Hampshire Tech Alliance says it was first presented in 1988 and recognises technology entrepreneurs based on factors including risk, innovation, growth, competition, profitability and employment.Grewal's selection reflects both his earlier work in networking and his more recent efforts in autonomous and electric systems. The Tech Alliance highlighted his decision to establish ePropelled's headquarters and manufacturing operations in New Hampshire and continue investing in local jobs and facilities as the company grows.His career also illustrates how technology sectors have changed since the 1980s and 1990s. Grewal's first major success was tied to computer networking at a time when businesses were building the infrastructure that would underpin modern internet connectivity. Decades later, his focus has shifted toward systems that combine electric propulsion, energy management and autonomy.Today, ePropelled's work spans aerospace, defence, maritime, industrial and autonomous systems markets. The company says it is developing technologies designed to improve the efficiency, endurance and performance of uncrewed platforms.For Grewal, the latest award marks a new milestone in a career that has already crossed several technology eras: from networking hardware and a Cisco acquisition in the 1990s to electric propulsion and autonomous vehicles in the 2020s.
Article Summary: Nick Grewal received the 2026 Entrepreneur of the Year Award from the New Hampshire Tech Alliance. The recognition follows a career spanning networking technology, investments in high-tech companies, and, more recently, electric propulsion systems for uncrewed vehicles. Before turning his attention to autonomous systems, he founded Nashoba Networks, a company Cisco acquired in 1996.

Article Title: Dawn Chaney was a three-sport athlete at Texas Woman's University in the 1960s; decades later, she gave $10 million for a new athletics complex
Article Text:
Dawn Chaney(on the right). Image Credit: Texas Woman’s University

What shaped Dawn Chaney’s connection with Texas Woman’s University

Texas Woman's University will build a $30 million athletics complex, which has been supplemented by a $10 million donation. Image Credit: Connor Pittman/Community Impact

Her career became a foundation for philanthropy

School of Health Promotion & Kinesiology. Image Credit: Texas Woman’s University

What will the new athletics complex provide

The project reflects a wider rise in Pioneer athletics

Chaney’s wider TWU legacy continues to grow

Dawn Chaney’s connection with Texas Woman’s University began as a student-athlete in the 1960s and has now grown into one of the university’s largest philanthropic legacies. A three-sport competitor during her time at TWU, Chaney later built a career in higher education and real estate. In 2026, she committed $10 million towards a new athletics complex that will carry her name. The approximately $30 million facility is expected to break ground in 2027, giving the university a new space designed around the needs of its growing athletics programme.Chaney’s relationship with Texas Woman’s University stretches across three degrees and several decades. According to TWU’s Pioneer Scholarship System, she is a three-time alumna of the university and earned degrees connected with kinesiology. The university’s July 2026 announcement also notes that she was a three-sport athlete during the 1960s, making her later support for athletics closely connected to her own experience as a student.Her professional life eventually moved beyond sport. As reported by TWU in 2022, Chaney spent 17 years teaching in higher education, working at institutions including Texas A&I University, the State University of New York, the University of Delaware and Bennett College in Greensboro, North Carolina.She later entered real estate investment and developed Chaney Properties.Chaney’s work in property development grew from a single-family property she acquired when she started Chaney Properties in 1980, according to the university’s scholarship profile. The business later expanded into single-family, multi-family, commercial, industrial and warehouse properties, with a particular focus on historic properties around downtown Greensboro.Her connection with TWU also remained active. The university’s 2022 report states that Chaney gave $100,000 to establish two $50,000 scholarship endowments for undergraduate and graduate students. The awards were intended to support students studying exercise physiology and exercise science, as well as students committed to women’s leadership.The Pioneer Scholarship System records those as the Dr. Dawn S. Chaney Undergraduate Scholarship Endowment and the Dr. Dawn S. Chaney Graduate Scholarship Endowment. They support students in the School of Health Promotion and Kinesiology, with preference for exercise science students and those demonstrating financial need.The planned facility is designed to address practical pressures created by the growth of TWU athletics. The university says its varsity sports programme expanded from 5 sports to 9 over six years, while the number of student-athletes more than doubled. That growth has placed greater demand on existing training and support spaces.According to TWU’s 2026 announcement, student-athletes currently share Pioneer Hall with academic kinesiology programmes. This has contributed to scheduling conflicts, crowded training areas and limited practice opportunities. Growing teams have also increased demand for locker rooms, weight-training areas and sports medicine facilities.The proposed 30,000- to 35,000-square-foot complex is intended to separate those functions and provide more room for athletes. Planned facilities include an auxiliary practice gym, locker rooms for five teams, a larger weight room capable of accommodating up to 40 athletes at once and a sports medicine clinic staffed by certified athletic trainers.The building is being planned at a time when TWU’s teams have been achieving notable results. The university reports 5 conference championships, 3 regional championships and 5 national championships during the recent period of expansion. Its athletics programme has also received three consecutive conference Academic Excellence Awards, along with the 2025 NCAA Division II President’s Award for Academic Excellence.Community Impact’s report on the planned $30 million facility places the project within this broader expansion of the university’s athletics programme. The new building is intended not only to provide additional training space but also to give the programme room to accommodate future growth.TWU also expects improved facilities to support activities beyond regular competition. The university has identified summer camps, youth programming and community engagement as areas that have been constrained by existing space.The $10 million athletics gift is not Chaney’s first major contribution to the university. TWU says the new commitment brings her into its top 5 donors and adds to earlier support that includes two kinesiology scholarships, the Chaney West Commons in the Health Sciences Center and founding support for the Texas Woman’s Athletics Hall of Fame.The new athletics complex will bear Chaney’s name as a result of the $10 million commitment, according to TWU. The university expects construction to begin in 2027.
Article Summary: Texas Woman's University will build a $30 million athletics complex, which has been supplemented by a $10 million donation. The planned facility is designed to address practical pressures created by the growth of TWU athletics. Planned facilities include an auxiliary practice gym, locker rooms for five teams, a larger weight room capable of accommodating up to 40 athletes at once.

Article Title: In 2003, a New York woman pulled a painting from trash on Manhattan’s Upper West Side; four years later she learned it was a stolen Rufino Tamayo work, and Sotheby’s sold it for $1,049,000
Article Text:
"Tres Personajes" by Mexican artist Rufi

The 1987 stealing

Discovering the identity

Rufino Tamayo and ‘ Tres Personajes ’

In 2003, Elizabeth Gibson was taking a morning walk on Manhattan’s Upper West Side when she noticed a brightly coloured abstract painting lying in the trash. She did not know who had painted it or why it had been thrown away. Still, something about the work made her stop and take it with her.Gibson later began looking into the painting she had found. Her search eventually led her to the website of “Antiques Roadshow FYI”, a companion programme to the PBS show “Antiques Roadshow”, CBC news reported. That was when she discovered that the painting was not an ordinary piece of discarded artwork.The painting was identified as “Tres Personajes” (Three People), a 1970 work by Mexican artist Rufino Tamayo. It had been bought by a Houston couple at Sotheby’s in 1977 and was stolen from a warehouse in 1987 while the couple were moving.The discovery came four years after Gibson had found the painting. Sotheby’s was preparing to sell the work at its Latin American Art auction on November 20, 2007. The auction house estimated that it could fetch up to $1 million.The Houston couple had bought “Tres Personajes” at Sotheby’s in 1977.The painting is an oil on canvas, with marble dust and sand worked into the paint. According to August Uribe, Sotheby’s senior vice president of Impressionist and modern art, the husband had paid $55,000 for it as a gift for his wife.The painting was kept in a warehouse while the couple were moving. It was stolen from the warehouse in 1987. The couple then reported the theft to Houston and federal authorities.Information about the missing painting was also entered into databases maintained by the International Foundation for Art Research and the Art Loss Register. Despite those efforts, there were no credible leads about where the work had gone.The painting eventually turned up in a completely different setting. Gibson found it lying in rubbish on a street in Manhattan, apparently unaware that it was a valuable work that had been missing for years.For Gibson, the discovery was not simply about finding an unusual painting. She said she immediately felt that the artwork had some importance, even though she did not understand why.“I would say it was an appointment with destiny,” Gibson said in a telephone interview with the Los Angeles Times. “I just knew it meant something. It was extremely powerful, and even though I didn’t understand it. I knew it had power,” she added.Gibson's search for information about the painting eventually connected her to “Antiques Roadshow FYI”. Uribe had featured “Tres Personajes” on the programme’s “Missing Masterpieces” segment.That helped Gibson realise that the painting she had taken from the rubbish was the same work that had been stolen from the Houston couple two decades earlier.By then, Tamayo's work had become highly valuable. Sotheby’s described “Tres Personajes” as an important work from the artist’s mature period and prepared it for the upcoming auction.The original owner, whose husband had since died, was putting the painting up for sale. The couple had also offered a $15,000 reward for information leading to the recovery of the stolen work.Gibson was due to receive that $15,000 reward. She was also set to receive an undisclosed percentage of the eventual sale price.Tamayo was born in 1899 in the Mexican state of Oaxaca. He studied at Mexico’s School of Fine Arts and began his career with work that had similarities to the style of well-known Mexican muralists such as Diego Rivera.His later work became more individual. It included vivid colours and expressions associated with Oaxaca, along with influences from pre-Columbian art.“Tres Personajes” reflected this later period of his career. Sotheby’s considered the 1970 painting an important example of Tamayo’s mature work.Tamayo became internationally known during his lifetime. He received numerous prizes and exhibited his work in the United States, South America, Europe and Russia. He died in 1991, but his paintings continued to attract strong interest.
Article Summary: 'Tres Personajes' by Mexican artist Rufino Tamayo was stolen in 1987. It had been bought by a Houston couple at Sotheby’s in 1977 and was stolen from a warehouse in 1987 while the couple were moving. Elizabeth Gibson found it lying in rubbish on a street in Manhattan in 2003 and took it home.

Article Title: A 1920-era American elm survived a 4,000-pound bomb in Oklahoma City; it was nearly cut down to recover evidence before becoming the Survivor Tree

How did the 1920-era elm survive changes in downtown Oklahoma City

How did the 1995 bombing change the story of the old elm

Why were plans to remove the elm abandoned after the bombing

From downtown tree to Oklahoma City’s Survivor Tree

The elm survived through decades of change as Oklahoma City’s downtown landscape continued to evolve.The elm had stood in downtown Oklahoma City as the city around it changed. Article Title: Priscilla Chan’s fund gave $330,000 to Kauaʻi schools; all 23 public and charter schools received flexible grants for the new academic year
Article Text:
Priscilla Chan’s $330,000 Kauaʻi schools funding gives all 23 schools flexibility

Priscilla Chan’s fund helps Kumu’s Cupboard provide free school supplies

Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi fund continues its community support for schools

Priscilla Chan’s fund extends Kauaʻi school support through free supplies

$330,000 from Priscilla Chan’s fund reaches all 23 Kauaʻi schools

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of school funding do you find most important? Supplies for students Teacher resources Facility improvements Technology upgrades 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Priscilla Chan’s fund has provided $330,000 to support Kauaʻi’s schools as the new academic year gets underway, with all 23 public and charter schools receiving a share of the funding. The unrestricted grants give school leaders flexibility to direct the money towards their most pressing needs. As reported by Hawaii News Now, the support also extends to Kumu’s Cupboard, a Līhuʻe nonprofit that provides free classroom supplies to teachers. The latest funding continues the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund’s support for the island, established in 2019. Separately, Chan and Mark Zuckerberg have also backed a free back-to-school event that distributed more than 3,000 supply-filled backpacks to local students.The latest grants cover Kauaʻi’s full public and charter school network, including 16 public schools and seven public charter schools. Rather than being tied to a particular classroom project or a narrowly defined expense, the funding is unrestricted.That gives individual school leaders room to decide how the money should be used. Needs can differ from one school to another, and flexible funding allows those decisions to be made locally rather than according to a single island-wide spending plan.Kauaʻi Complex Area Superintendent Leila Maeda-Kobayashi said, “Unrestricted or flexible grants empower our school leaders to direct resources exactly where they are needed most.”For schools preparing for a new academic year, that flexibility can matter. Expenses are not always the same from one campus to the next, and unrestricted support can be directed towards practical requirements as they arise.The funding is not limited to schools themselves. Kumu’s Cupboard, based in Līhuʻe, is also among the recipients. The nonprofit provides classroom supplies free of charge to teachers and other educational staff throughout the year. Its role is separate from the individual schools, but its work is closely connected to the day-to-day costs educators can face when putting together lessons and classroom activities.Including the organisation in the grant distribution broadens the reach of the funding beyond school campuses. It also means teachers can access supplies through a community organisation rather than relying solely on resources allocated to their schools.The Chan Zuckerberg Kauai Community Fund was established in 2019 as a way of supporting community needs on the island. The fund operates through the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation, which administers the latest grants.The new distribution comes at the beginning of the 2026-27 school year, when schools, families and educators are again dealing with the costs associated with returning to class. Hawaiʻi Community Foundation Program Director Marissa Sandblom said, “By addressing resource disparities and financial pressures facing students, families, and educators, we can help remove barriers and cultivate the necessary conditions for meaningful engagement in learning. ”The decision to provide unrestricted grants is significant in practical terms because schools can determine where the money is most useful rather than receiving funding that can only be spent on a predetermined programme.The fund's support has also extended into a community back-to-school event. Reportedly, Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg joined other local donors in sponsoring Kukui Grove’s Back to School Bash. The event is described by organisers as Kauaʻi’s largest free school supply giveaway. More than 3,000 backpacks, each filled with school supplies, were distributed to K-12 students. That initiative provides a more direct form of assistance for families. While the school grants are managed at an institutional level, the giveaway puts supplies directly into the hands of students preparing to return to classrooms.Taken together, the two forms of support cover different parts of the school community. The grants give schools and an education-focused nonprofit greater control over resources, while the giveaway helps students with some of the basic supplies needed for the new school year.The scale of the latest funding is partly defined by its coverage. All 23 public and charter schools on Kauaʻi are included, rather than a selected group of campuses. It also reflects the fund’s wider community focus, which has continued since its establishment in 2019.For the schools receiving the unrestricted grants, the next step is deciding how that money can best be used locally. For Kumu’s Cupboard, the funding adds support for its ongoing supply programme. And for the thousands of students who received backpacks at the Back to School Bash, the benefit was more immediate: school materials to take with them as classes began.
Article Summary: $330,000 from Priscilla Chan’s fund reaches all 23 Kauaʻi schools. The unrestricted grants give school leaders flexibility to direct the money towards their most pressing needs. The support also extends to Kumu's Cupboard, a Līhuʻe nonprofit that provides free classroom supplies to teachers.

Article Title: Texas man faces execution for killing convenience store clerk in 2000
Article Text:
Texas man to be executed for killing convenience store clerk in 2000

A Texas man convicted of killing a convenience store clerk in 2000 is set to be executed by lethal injection on Wednesday. If carried out, it would be the 30th execution in the US this year.Jamaal Howard, 46, was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Vickie Swartout, 42. She was shot once in the chest during a robbery at a store in Silsbee, a small town about 161 km northeast of Houston.Howard was 20 when the killing took place. According to court records cited by news agency Associated Press, he took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store. Surveillance video presented during the trial showed Howard shooting Swartout.Howard's lawyers have argued that he is intellectually disabled and should not be executed. The state has argued that he has not provided enough evidence to support the claim.Howard has also asked the US Supreme Court to stop the execution.The Supreme Court barred the execution of people with intellectual disabilities in 2002, but allowed states some discretion in deciding whether a person meets the criteria.If Howard's execution goes ahead, he will be the seventh person executed in Texas this year. Two more executions are currently scheduled in the state.The execution would come after a failed attempt last week to execute Christa Pike in Tennessee. Pike's lawyers said on Tuesday that she remained awake and was speaking while receiving treatment at a hospital.
Article Summary: Jamaal Howard, 46, was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Vickie Swartout, 42. She was shot once in the chest during a robbery at a store in Silsbee, Texas. Howard's lawyers have argued that he is intellectually disabled and should not be executed.

Article Title: Texas ranchers blocked well operators from a 1,604-acre tract in 2004; on October 1, an appeals court ruled an oil company may cross the land to plug a shut-in well 15 to 20 yards from the San Antonio
Article Text:
Texas ranchers blocked well operators from 1,604 acres in 2004; court lets oil firm cross property (Image Credit: McFaddin Ranch)

A dispute over access to a well

Why Allegiant wanted to cross the ranch

The landowners refused access

What the appeals court decided

A ranch with a long South Texas history

What the ruling means
